analysis.one_liner: Bans employers from permanently replacing workers who go on strike.
analysis.headline: The House passed the striker-replacement ban 239-190, but the Senate never voted and the bill died when the 103rd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change federal labor law so employers cannot fire striking workers by hiring permanent replacements, and cannot deny returning strikers their old jobs or other benefits in favor of those replacements. It would apply to most private workplaces under the National Labor Relations Act and to railroads and airlines under the Railway Labor Act. Employers could still hire temporary workers during a strike, just not permanently keep replacements in a striker's job.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who strike or organize a union. Under current law an employer can permanently replace a striker and lawfully keep the replacement afterward, so striking means risking your job for good. This bill would make that an illegal unfair labor practice, letting workers strike for better wages and conditions without losing their livelihood, and guaranteeing returning strikers their jobs ahead of anyone who did the work during the dispute [S2][S5].

how_it_helps.text: Makes it an illegal unfair labor practice for an employer to promise, threaten, or take action to hire a permanent replacement for an employee in a unionized bargaining unit who is striking or engaging in collective action through the union [S2][S5].
Bars employers from denying a returning striker their job or any other employment right or privilege out of preference for someone who crossed the picket line or was willing to [S2][S5].
Applies the same ban to railroads and airlines under the Railway Labor Act, covering the industries where long, high-stakes strikes are most common [S2][S5].
The bill carried broad early support: 195 cosponsors, including 192 of the House's Democrats and its two Independent members, and it passed the House 239-190 [S6][S8].

analysis.who_pays: Employers, who would lose the ability to permanently restaff with replacements during a strike. Businesses argued this shifts bargaining leverage toward unions, raises the cost of resisting union wage demands, and could mean longer strikes that disrupt operations before a settlement; those costs could partly reach consumers through prices [S2].
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers facing strikes and union drives

drawbacks.text: The bill protects workers only within its defined categories: it covers employees in bargaining units with a certified union, or units where a union petition for an election based on majority authorization is pending with the labor board, and who act through that union [S2][S5].

The honest cost: taking permanent replacement off the table strengthens unions' leverage in a strike. Employers facing a walkout would have to keep jobs open for strikers indefinitely rather than restructure, and businesses argued settlements and prices would rise as a result [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the workers covered, the benefit is concrete and large: the right to strike without permanently losing your job, which is the single biggest risk a unionized worker takes in a dispute. The cost falls on employers during labor disputes, in the form of reduced leverage and the possibility of longer strikes before settlement. How much of that cost spreads to the broader public through prices is debated, but it is real to the employers who bear it. The bill was narrowly drawn and did not ban replacements outright, only permanent ones, which limits the disruption critics feared.

outcome.mechanism: It passed the House but the Senate let it sit on its calendar without ever holding a vote, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced on January 5, 1993 by Rep. William Clay with 195 cosponsors, the bill was sent to three House committees (Education and Labor, Energy and Commerce, and Public Works and Transportation), which held hearings and reported it in late May and early June 1993; the Labor Department submitted favorable comment [S6][S7].
The House passed the bill on June 15, 1993 by 239 to 190, with Democrats voting 221-33 for it and Republicans voting 157-17 against [S8].

The Senate received the bill on June 16 and placed it on its legislative calendar on June 22, 1993. No committee action, debate, or vote ever followed, and the bill expired at the end of the 103rd Congress on January 3, 1995 [S7].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers, who kept the legal ability to permanently replace striking workers, and the senators who opposed the ban without ever having to cast a public vote on it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers, and senators who avoided a vote

for.name: Rep. William (Bill) Clay
for.role: Sponsor, House Education and Labor Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and steered it through committee markup and House passage.

for.name: 192 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill and supplied 221 of its 239 votes on final passage.

for.name: Department of Labor
for.what_they_did: Submitted favorable executive comment on the bill during committee consideration.

for.name: Organized labor (AFL-CIO and allied unions)
for.what_they_did: Made the striker-replacement ban their top legislative priority of 1993 and pressed for House and Senate passage.

against.name: 157 House Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted no on final passage, 157-17, and moved to recommit the bill to committee (the motion failed on a voice vote).

against.name: 33 House Democrats
against.what_they_did: Voted against the bill on final passage.

against.name: U.S. Chamber of Commerce and employer associations
against.what_they_did: Opposed the ban as an unfair tilt of strike leverage toward unions and lobbied against it in the House and Senate.

against.name: Senate Republican filibuster
against.what_they_did: Blocked the companion Senate strike-replacement bill later in 1993 with a filibuster that failed to reach the 60 votes needed to end debate, and the House-passed bill never received a Senate vote.

sides.party_line_note: Passage split sharply by party: Democrats voted 221-33 for the bill while Republicans voted 17-157 for it, with the yes total of 239 falling short of what was needed to survive a likely Senate filibuster.

industries.industry: Employers in unionized industries (manufacturing, transport, services)
industries.note: The bill removes their main legal weapon in a strike — permanently replacing the workforce — which business groups said would raise the cost of settling disputes and shift leverage to unions. For workers, that weapon is the reason striking can mean losing your job for good.

Unions made the striker-replacement ban their top legislative priority because the threat of permanent replacement has hollowed out the strike as a tool; banning it strengthens every future organizing drive and negotiation. Union strength in bargaining flows directly to their members' wages and conditions.

The bill amends the Railway Labor Act, which governs these carriers, to bar granting permanent replacement status or job preferences to people who worked during a dispute. These carriers' strikes most disrupt the traveling public, so the leverage shift is most visible here.
